meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'sofa, couch' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Better than our sofa!
He is sitting on the sofa.
I will reach the sofa myself.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Юле бы дублёнку купили, Славику бы ноутбук.
examples.trans: We could have bought Yulia a sheepskin coat, and Slavik a laptop.
Look who's talking.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'вести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to bring, lead'.

examples.trans: You will bring the child in the morning.

examples.text: Нужно срочно привести его в человеческий вид!
examples.trans: He must urgently be brought into a presentable state!

examples.text: Они привели нового шеф-повара прямо из Индии.
examples.trans: They brought a new chef straight from India.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

examples.text: Мы сюда зачем прилетели? Я сразу сказал: с ним ничего не получится.
examples.trans: What did we even fly out here for? I said from the start: nothing will come of it with him.
Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('splendid, luxurious').

examples.trans: It is a magnificent couch.

examples.text: Сегодня у шефа очень шикарный день в ресторане.
examples.trans: Today the chef is having a very splendid day at the restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'my, mine', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
That's mine.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: From French 'cabinet' (private study or office).

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, я сейчас в кабинете у мэра.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, I'm in the mayor's office right now.
Please leave the office!

examples.text: В кабинете мэра была скрытая камера.
examples.trans: In the mayor's office there was a hidden camera.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

examples.text: А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very, very much', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
It's very hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'добно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Very convenient.

examples.text: На кухне все стараются работать удобно.
examples.trans: In the kitchen everyone tries to work comfortable.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nobody', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Nobody will come in.
I know the town like nobody else.

examples.text: Садитесь и держите дверь. Никто не войдёт.
examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door. Nobody will come in.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no; there isn't', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, it's mine.
No? All right.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.
See the markers? They're from Japan!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

молчать.gloss: to be silent, to say nothing

meanings.en: to be silent, to say nothing
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be silent, to say nothing', paired with 'замолчать'.

examples.trans: Why aren't you saying anything?

examples.text: Ну что ты молчишь? Ты толстый, ты не спортсмен!
examples.trans: Well, why are you so quiet? You're fat, you're no athlete!
All right, sit there, eat and be quiet.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'all right, OK', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: All right, here you go.
OK, I'm coming.
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'частвовать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to participate, to take part'.

examples.trans: I am taking part in the election.

examples.text: Как вы знаете, Виталий, я участвую в выборах.
examples.trans: As you know, Vitaly, I am taking part in the election.

examples.text: Но я в этих махинациях не участвовал!
examples.trans: But I did not participate in these schemes!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.
This is for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'отрудник'). Derived noun with agent/object suffix '-ник'/'-щик'/'-чик'. Common masculine noun meaning 'employee, staff member' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Why are you mistreating our staff?
All staff members gathered in the conference hall.
Now all employees will suffer.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'дельный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('separate').

examples.trans: A separate room.

examples.text: У меня есть отдельная комната в коммуналке.
examples.trans: I have a separate room in a communal flat.

examples.text: У меня есть две отдельные комнаты.
examples.trans: I have two separate rooms.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'анузел'). Common masculine noun meaning 'restroom, bathroom' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: There is a separate restroom for staff members.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новый санузел.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new restroom.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'matter; thing to do' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I have a lot to do.
How are things?

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'hello'.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?
Arkady Borisovich, hello.
Hello, Arkady Borisovich.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine there.
Who's there?
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лива'). Common feminine noun meaning 'plum' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I stepped in a rotten plum.

examples.text: Я наступил в гнилую сливу, шеф.
examples.trans: I stepped in a rotten plum, chef.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ломаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to break down, get broken', paired with 'ломаться'.

examples.trans: My tank broke.
Yesterday the washing machine broke down.
This stupid machine simply broke.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Grab him!
It needs a wash.
Four-eyes! Grab him!
